title: Fourier Series
summary: A Fourier series writes a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines. We need it to fit initial conditions in PDEs. The eigenfunctions of Chapter 6 are exactly these sines and cosines.

intro.x: A Fourier series writes a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines. We need it to fit initial conditions in PDEs. The eigenfunctions of Chapter 6 are exactly these sines and cosines.

blocks.x: Let $f$ be periodic with period $2L$. Its Fourier series is
f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\Big(a_n\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L} + b_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\Big),
with coefficients
a_n = \frac1L\int_{-L}^{L}f(x)\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x \ (n\ge0), \qquad b_n = \frac1L\int_{-L}^{L}f(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x \ (n\ge1).
These formulas come from orthogonality (Chapter 6). Multiply both sides by $\cos(m\pi x/L)$ or $\sin(m\pi x/L)$, integrate over one period, and all terms but one vanish.

Assume $f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum\big(a_n\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L} + b_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\big)$ and that we may integrate term by term. We need these integrals over one period, for integers $m,n\ge1$:
\int_{-L}^{L}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = 0,\qquad \int_{-L}^{L}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = 0,

\int_{-L}^{L}\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = \begin{cases}L & m=n\\0 & m\ne n\end{cases},\qquad \int_{-L}^{L}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = \begin{cases}L & m=n\\0 & m\ne n\end{cases},
\int_{-L}^{L}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = 0\ \text{ for all } m,n.
They follow from $\cos A\cos B = \frac12[\cos(A-B)+\cos(A+B)]$, $\sin A\sin B = \frac12[\cos(A-B)-\cos(A+B)]$ and $\sin A\cos B = \frac12[\sin(A+B)+\sin(A-B)]$, exactly as in Chapter 6.
Find $a_0$. Integrate the series over $(-L,L)$. Every term vanishes except the constant: $\int_{-L}^{L}f\,\dd x = \frac{a_0}{2}\cdot2L$, so $a_0 = \frac1L\int_{-L}^{L}f\,\dd x$.

Find $a_m$. Multiply the series by $\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}$ and integrate over $(-L,L)$. Only the term $a_m\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}$ survives, and it gives $a_m\cdot L$. So $a_m = \frac1L\int_{-L}^{L}f(x)\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$.
Find $b_m$. Multiply by $\sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}$ and integrate: $b_m = \frac1L\int_{-L}^{L}f(x)\sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$.
The formula for $a_n$ with $n=0$ would give twice the constant term. This is why the constant term is written as $a_0/2$.

If $f$ is piecewise smooth on one period (finite number of jumps and finite number of maxima and minima), then the series converges. At every point where $f$ is continuous the sum equals $f(x)$. At a jump, the sum equals the average of the left and right limits.
If $f$ is even ($f(-x)=f(x)$): all $b_n = 0$, and $a_n = \dfrac2L\displaystyle\int_0^L f(x)\cos\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$. We get a cosine series.
If $f$ is odd ($f(-x)=-f(x)$): all $a_n=0$, and $b_n = \dfrac2L\displaystyle\int_0^L f(x)\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$. We get a sine series.
Check for even or odd first. It saves half the work.

blocks.name: Derivation
blocks.title: Even and odd functions, and half-range series

blocks.x: Odd $f$. Then $f(x)\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}$ is (odd)$\times$(even) $=$ odd, and the integral of an odd function over $(-L,L)$ is zero. So $a_n = 0$. The product $f(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$ is even, so $\int_{-L}^{L} = 2\int_0^L$, and $b_n = \frac2L\int_0^Lf\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$.
Even $f$. In the same way $b_n = 0$ and $a_n = \frac2L\int_0^Lf\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$.

Half-range series. Given $f$ only on $(0,L)$, define $f_{\text{odd}}(-x) = -f(x)$ and $f_{\text{even}}(-x) = f(x)$ on $(-L,0)$. Each extension is a function on $(-L,L)$ with its own Fourier series (a sine series for the odd one and a cosine series for the even one). On $(0,L)$ both series equal the original $f$.
$f(x) = -1$ on $(-\pi, 0)$ and $f(x)=1$ on $(0,\pi)$, period $2\pi$ (so $L=\pi$).
$f$ is odd, so $a_n = 0$ and
b_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi \sin nx\,\dd x = \frac{2}{\pi}\cdot\frac{1 - \cos n\pi}{n} = \begin{cases}\dfrac{4}{n\pi} & n \text{ odd},\\[4pt] 0 & n\text{ even}.\end{cases}
f(x) = \frac4\pi\Big(\sin x + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} + \frac{\sin 5x}{5} + \cdots\Big).
At the jump $x=0$ the series gives $0$, the average of $-1$ and $1$.
Figure: partial sums of the square-wave series. More terms follow the wave better, but there is always an overshoot of about 9% near the jump (Gibbs phenomenon).

$f$ is odd. $b_n = \dfrac2\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\sin nx\,\dd x$. Integrate by parts: $\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\sin nx\,\dd x = \Big[-\frac{x\cos nx}{n} + \frac{\sin nx}{n^2}\Big]_0^\pi = -\frac{\pi\cos n\pi}{n}$. So
b_n = -\frac{2\cos n\pi}{n} = \frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}{n}, \qquad x = 2\Big(\sin x - \frac{\sin 2x}{2} + \frac{\sin 3x}{3} - \cdots\Big).
$f$ is even. $a_0 = \dfrac2\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x^2\,\dd x = \dfrac{2\pi^2}{3}$. For $n\ge1$,
a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2\cos nx\,\dd x = \frac2\pi\Big[\frac{x^2\sin nx}{n} + \frac{2x\cos nx}{n^2} - \frac{2\sin nx}{n^3}\Big]_0^\pi = \frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}.
x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx.
A bonus. Put $x = \pi$: $\pi^2 = \dfrac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum\dfrac1{n^2}$, so $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$.
Suppose $f$ is given only on $(0,L)$ (a rod or a string). We can extend it to $(-L,0)$ in two ways, and each choice gives a different series for the same $f$ on $(0,L)$.
Sine series (odd extension): $f(x) = \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$,   $b_n = \dfrac2L\displaystyle\int_0^L f(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$.
Cosine series (even extension): $f(x) = \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}$,   $a_n = \dfrac2L\displaystyle\int_0^L f(x)\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x$.
Use the sine series when the PDE has zero values at the ends ($u=0$). Use the cosine series when the ends are insulated ($u_x=0$).

$a_0 = \dfrac2\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\pi x\,\dd x = \pi$. For $n\ge1$: $a_n = \dfrac2\pi\Big[\dfrac{x\sin nx}{n} + \dfrac{\cos nx}{n^2}\Big]_0^\pi = \dfrac{2\big((-1)^n - 1\big)}{\pi n^2}$, which is $-\dfrac{4}{\pi n^2}$ for odd $n$ and $0$ for even $n$.
x = \frac\pi2 - \frac4\pi\Big(\cos x + \frac{\cos 3x}{9} + \frac{\cos 5x}{25} + \cdots\Big),\qquad 0<x<\pi.
Check at $x=0$: $0 = \dfrac\pi2 - \dfrac4\pi\cdot\dfrac{\pi^2}{8} = 0$. ✓
The energy of $f$ equals the sum of the energies of its harmonics:
\frac1L\int_{-L}^{L}\big[f(x)\big]^2\,\dd x = \frac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\big(a_n^2 + b_n^2\big).

Multiply the series $f = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum(a_n\cos + b_n\sin)$ by $f$ itself and integrate over $(-L,L)$. By Euler’s formulas, $\int f\,\dd x = La_0$, $\int f\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = La_n$ and $\int f\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = Lb_n$. So
\int_{-L}^{L}f^2\,\dd x = \frac{a_0}{2}\,(La_0) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty\big(a_n\cdot La_n + b_n\cdot Lb_n\big).
Divide by $L$ to get $\dfrac1L\displaystyle\int_{-L}^{L}f^2\,\dd x = \dfrac{a_0^2}{2} + \sum\big(a_n^2 + b_n^2\big)$.
For the square wave: the left side is $\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}1\,\dd x = 2$. The right side is $\sum_{n\text{ odd}}\frac{16}{\pi^2n^2} = \frac{16}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^2}{8} = 2$. ✓
Find the Fourier series of $f(x)=|x|$ on $(-\pi,\pi)$.
Find the Fourier series of $f(x)=x$ on $(-1,1)$ (period 2, so $L=1$).
Find the half-range sine series of $f(x) = 1$ on $(0,L)$.
Use the series of $x^2$ at $x=0$ to find $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$.
To what value does the square-wave series converge at $x=0$ and at $x=\pi/2$?

(1) Even. $a_0 = \pi$, $a_n = \dfrac{2((-1)^n - 1)}{\pi n^2}$: $|x| = \dfrac\pi2 - \dfrac4\pi\Big(\cos x + \dfrac{\cos 3x}{9} + \cdots\Big)$.   (2) $f = \dfrac2\pi\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}\sin n\pi x$.   (3) $b_n = \dfrac{2}{L}\displaystyle\int_0^L\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}\,\dd x = \dfrac{2(1-(-1)^n)}{n\pi}$, so $f = \dfrac4\pi\displaystyle\sum_{n\text{ odd}}\dfrac1n\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}$.   (4) $0 = \frac{\pi^2}{3} + 4\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$, so $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2} = -\frac{\pi^2}{12}$ and the answer is $\dfrac{\pi^2}{12}$.   (5) At $x = 0$ (a jump) it converges to $0$. At $x=\pi/2$ (continuous) it converges to $1$.
